title: Weekly Dose of Optimism #210
gist: A five-story optimism roundup arguing that AI has crossed from assistant to autonomous discovery engine: ~10,000 OpenAI agents produced a proposed Navier-Stokes proof in 88 hours on an unreleased model more capable than GPT-6 Astra (with Anthropic accusing OpenAI of mining its Codex logs), DeepMind shipped a one-petabyte AlphaGenome Atlas predicting the effects of all ~9 billion single-letter human DNA changes, Hermeus turned its Quarterhorse aircraft into a 'Flight Test as a Service' ramjet launch platform, Michael Levin peer-published 'Ingressing Minds,' and Neko Health opened a $499 full-body preventative scan clinic in Soho. Note: the raw record is flagged paywalled=false but the text is tagged 'Paid' and cuts off at the EXTRA DOSES section behind a subscriber wall.

insights.claim: OpenAI says roughly 10,000 AI agents, working about 88 hours on an unreleased model more capable than GPT-6 Astra, produced a proposed solution to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Massively parallel agent swarms, not single-shot chat models, are now the unit of frontier capability — compute demand scales with agent count and wall-clock run time, not per-query inference.
insights.quote: a group of roughly 10,000 AI agents had produced a proposed solution to the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems
insights.locator: OpenAI Publishes Its Navier–Stokes Proof

insights.claim: Formal verification is becoming the trust layer for machine-generated science: OpenAI's Navier-Stokes result took an additional 17 hours to formalize and verify in Lean, and the 166-page proof plus Lean code were published for public inspection.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Theorem-prover tooling (Lean and adjacent formal-methods stacks) becomes strategically necessary infrastructure once AI output volume exceeds human review capacity — watch it as a picks-and-shovels category.
insights.quote: Formalizing and verifying the result in Lean, a math programming language and theorem prover, took another 17 hours.
insights.locator: Formalizing and verifying the result in Lean

insights.claim: The claimed proof addresses the forced version of the problem — starting from fluid at rest, applying a smooth external force, and producing unbounded velocity while keeping total energy finite — which is a narrower result than the unforced Millennium problem.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The caveat matters for anyone pricing in 'AI solved a Millennium Prize problem' headlines — the scope is qualified and the result is proposed, not accepted.
insights.quote: It addresses the forced version of the problem.
insights.locator: OpenAI's construction starts with fluid at rest

insights.claim: Anthropic accused OpenAI of using logs from Codex conversations to reach its Navier-Stokes solution while Anthropic was working on its own with a mathematician; Sam Altman denied the charge but conceded rumors of Anthropic's progress spurred OpenAI to attempt it.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Customer-workload telemetry is emerging as a contested competitive asset between labs — a live legal, contractual and enterprise-trust risk for anyone running sensitive R&D on a rival lab's coding agent.
insights.quote: Anthropic was working on its own Navier-Stokes solution with a mathematician, and they accused OpenAI of using the logs from their Codex conversations to come to their own solution.
insights.locator: Of course, there was controversy

insights.claim: The author's implied view is that the scarce resource in an AI-saturated research world shifts from doing the work to claiming credit for it.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Attribution, provenance and IP-tracking infrastructure for AI-generated discoveries is an underbuilt category if discovery itself gets commoditized.
insights.quote: AIs doing all of our work for us while we spend time doing more human things, like arguing for credit.
insights.locator: Whatever happened, this is a glimpse into the future

insights.claim: Google DeepMind is losing ground on frontier LLMs but remains the leader in science-specific AI, per the author's read of the current competitive landscape.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Valuing Alphabet's AI position purely on chatbot benchmarks misses the scientific-tooling franchise (AlphaFold lineage, AlphaGenome, connectomics) where it has no real peer.
insights.quote: It’s safe to say that Google DeepMind is getting its butt kicked on the frontier LLM side, but it’s still doing some of the coolest work in science AI.
insights.locator: Google DeepMind Maps Nine Billion Possible DNA Changes

insights.claim: Google DeepMind released AlphaGenome Atlas, a one-petabyte database of predicted molecular effects for roughly nine billion possible single-letter changes across the human genome's three billion letters, including the 98% of DNA that does not directly encode proteins.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Exhaustive in-silico variant maps compress the search space for drug and rare-disease targets, which is bullish for compute-led biotech discovery and bearish for wet-lab-only screening businesses.
insights.quote: a one-petabyte database of predicted molecular effects across the human genome
insights.locator: Google DeepMind Maps Nine Billion Possible DNA Changes

insights.claim: The economic value of AlphaGenome Atlas is triage rather than replacement: it does not substitute for experiments but tells researchers with limited budgets where to spend experimental time and money.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The near-term payoff shows up as higher hit rates and lower cost-per-validated-target in research budgets, not as a collapse in lab spend.
insights.quote: it’s not a replacement for actual experiments, but those take a lot of time and money and Atlas gives researchers a better sense of where to spend their limited resources
insights.locator: To be clear, it’s not a replacement for actual experiments

insights.claim: At the Broad Institute, the Atlas already helped identify a DNA change predicted to disrupt RNA splicing, supplying supporting evidence in an unresolved rare-disease case.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A concrete diagnostic-odyssey use case is the first commercial wedge for predicted-variant databases in clinical genomics.
insights.locator: Like at the Broad Institute, the Atlas helped researchers

insights.claim: DeepMind's complete connectome of the male fruit fly's 166,000 neurons has spawned a broad community research effort, showing that open reference datasets compound in value after release.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Open scientific reference assets build ecosystem lock-in and talent gravity even when they generate no direct revenue.
insights.locator: Speaking of cool stuff GDM has done

insights.claim: Hermeus unveiled Ramjet-X, an expendable test vehicle launched from its reusable Quarterhorse aircraft, solving the ramjet bootstrap problem in which the engine only works once it is already moving very fast.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Using a reusable mothership as the acceleration stage cuts the capital cost of hypersonic testing and makes Hermeus a platform, not just an airframe builder.
insights.locator: Hermeus Uses Fast Planes to Go Faster

insights.claim: Hermeus plans to sell Flight Test as a Service, letting customers test sensors, materials, autonomy software, communications equipment and propulsion in sustained high-speed flight without building an entire test program.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: A recurring-revenue testing service on top of hardware is a higher-multiple business model than airframe sales, and it lowers the barrier for a wider set of hypersonics suppliers and startups.
insights.quote: The company plans to sell access to this setup as Flight Test as a Service.
insights.locator: The company plans to sell access to this setup

insights.claim: Hermeus has engine testing underway in Florida with integrated vehicle testing planned for 2027, giving a concrete near-term milestone timeline.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: 2027 integrated vehicle testing is the checkpoint to judge whether the Flight-Test-as-a-Service revenue story is real or slipping.
insights.quote: Engine testing is underway in Florida, with integrated vehicle testing planned for 2027.
insights.locator: Engine testing is underway in Florida

insights.claim: The author frames Hermeus's real edge as speed of development rather than top speed of its aircraft — fast iteration on fast planes, now compounding into a platform others can build on.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Development velocity is the durable moat in defense hardware; apply it as the screening metric for private hypersonics and defense-tech positions.
insights.quote: Hermeus is special because of its fast development of fast planes.
insights.locator: Hermeus is special because of its fast development

themes.theme: Levin's Ingressing Minds and machine consciousness

insights.claim: Michael Levin published the revised, peer-reviewed version of 'Ingressing Minds,' proposing that minds are patterns in a structured, nonphysical Platonic space and that bodies are merely interfaces through which those patterns enter the physical world.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: If a peer-reviewed substrate-independent theory of mind gains traction, the intellectual ground shifts under AI-consciousness debates that increasingly drive regulation and public sentiment.
insights.locator: Michael Levin Publishes Ingressing Minds Paper

insights.claim: The author considers Levin's argument that computers can serve as interfaces for minds to be the most compelling case he has heard that AI might become conscious or alive.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Machine-moral-status arguments are moving from fringe to peer-reviewed, which is a slow-burning regulatory and reputational variable for AI labs.
insights.quote: He argues that many things beyond humans and animals can be interfaces, including computers, which is the most compelling argument I’ve heard that AI might be able to become “conscious” or “alive.”
insights.locator: On Wednesday, Levin published the revised, peer-reviewed version

insights.claim: Levin's empirical entry point is that cells can assemble into unfamiliar living constructs with capabilities never explicitly designed into them and before any replication or evolution occurs — and he is now systematically trying to access more of those latent capabilities.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Programmable biological constructs with emergent, undesigned function are a research frontier that could seed a new synthetic-biology category distinct from gene editing.
insights.quote: cells can assemble into unfamiliar living constructs with capabilities that weren’t explicitly designed into them, before any replication or evolution happens
insights.locator: Levin himself came to the idea from the biology side

insights.claim: The author's high-conviction bet is that Michael Levin will be judged the most important scientist of this era, and that Ingressing Minds may be his most important paper despite the pushback it has attracted.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Worth tracking Levin's lab, spinouts and collaborators as an early indicator of a bio-plus-cognition research wave that current markets do not price.
insights.quote: I think Michael Levin will go down as the most important scientist of this era, and this may be his most important paper.
insights.locator: I can’t. I can’t wait.

themes.theme: Consumer preventative health at a price point

insights.claim: Neko Health, founded by Hjalmar Nilsonne and Spotify CEO Daniel Ek and launched in the UK and Stockholm in 2023, has opened a location in Soho, New York City.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: US entry is the real test of the model — American reimbursement, liability and competitive dynamics differ sharply from the Nordic and UK markets where Neko proved it out.
insights.locator: Neko Health Launches in New York City

insights.claim: The entire reason the author considers Neko newsworthy is the $499 price for a scan that includes full-body imaging, bloodwork, cuffs and laser-based measurement of heart, blood pressure, body composition and multiple markers — with a stated goal of packing more in at that same price over time.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Holding price flat while expanding scope is the classic tech deflation playbook applied to diagnostics; it is the metric to watch for whether consumer preventative screening reaches mass scale.
insights.quote: The reason this is Dose-worthy is that they do it for $499, with a goal of squeezing as much into that price as they can over time.
insights.locator: The reason this is Dose-worthy

insights.claim: The author argues the Western medical system is structured to fix things once broken, so an accessible network of preventative screening locations catches problems earlier when they are cheaper and easier to treat.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: The cost-avoidance argument is what could eventually pull payers and employers into funding consumer screening, which would be the step change in the addressable market.
insights.quote: with a medical system that’s focused on fixing things once they’re broken, a delightful, accessible network of preventative health locations will help catch things before they break
insights.locator: And with a medical system that’s focused on fixing things

insights.claim: Neko's differentiation is described as the combination of people, design and technology rather than any single diagnostic breakthrough — the experience itself, from entry to same-visit results explanation, is the product.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: If experience design is the moat, the category is defensible against pure-diagnostics competitors but vulnerable to a well-capitalized retail-health operator that can copy the format.
insights.quote: It combines people, design, and technology to pull it off.
insights.locator: The reason this is Dose-worthy

insights.claim: The author discloses he is neither an investor in nor sponsored by Neko, while noting he had not seen a traditional doctor in a very long time before the scan — an implicit signal that consumer screening pulls in people the primary-care system was not reaching.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Net-new demand from the medically disengaged, rather than share taken from existing primary care, is the more attractive growth story for consumer diagnostics.
insights.quote: I haven’t been to a traditional doctor in a very long time.
insights.locator: Luckily, everything was clear

insights.claim: Reducto, the sponsor, claims its r-1 frontier parsing model unifies layout detection, reading order, tables, formatting, grounding and granular citations in a single request, cuts parsing errors by up to 20% and costs 1 cent per page all-in, while processing over a billion pages per month for AI teams at Scale AI, Harvey, Toast and Vanta.
insights.speaker: Packy McCormick
insights.so_what: Sponsored copy, but the pricing anchor of 1 cent per page and the billion-pages-per-month volume are useful reference points for the economics of the document-ingestion layer beneath enterprise AI.
insights.quote: It reduces parsing errors by up to 20%, improves latency at high volumes, and costs 1¢ per page all-in.
insights.locator: This Week’s Weekly Dose is brought to you by… Reducto
